nase will yield NADH and two substrate phosphorylation steps, phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase, are linked to the
synthesis of ATP. Since each three carbon unit yields 2 ATPs the total yield is 4 ATPs but because two ATPs were utilized in the ﬁrst
part of the pathway the net yield is two ATP per glucose plus two pyruvates and 2 NADH. To maintain ﬂux in the pathway, and to
keep using glucose, this NADH must be oxidized back to NADþ. In oxidative cells the reducing power of the NADH can be trans-
ferred to the mitochondria but if this is not possible the NADH will be used by lactate dehydrogenase to reduce the pyruvate to
lactate limiting the ATP yield to 2 per glucose metabolized. Sugars such as fructose and galactose can enter the glycolytic pathway
after being phosphorylated by speciﬁc isozymes of hexokinase and metabolized to intermediates, triose phosphates for fructose and
glucose 6 phosphate for galactose, that feed into the glycolytic pathway.
If however, the pyruvate is destined to be fully oxidized in the mitochondria then the NADH formed in the cytosol also must be
transferred to the mitochondria. The mitochondrial membrane, however, is impermeable to NAD and NADH and shuttles exist to
